analysis.one_liner: Expands the exemption from overtime pay for computer professionals to cover network and database workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to committee and then a subcommittee in May 2003 and died there when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires overtime pay (time-and-a-half after 40 hours a week) for most workers, but already carves out an exemption for some highly paid computer professionals. This bill would expand that exemption in the statute itself, covering computer network and database analysts, designers, and developers [S2][S3]. Workers who qualify would no longer be legally entitled to overtime pay; their employers would no longer owe it [S2][S3]. The bill never advanced past its first committee assignment [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers of technology workers, especially companies that employ network engineers, database administrators, and systems analysts earning $27.63 an hour or more (about $57,000 a year full-time). Those employers would no longer owe overtime pay to employees doing that work, giving them more flexibility to require long hours at straight time [S3]. The workers themselves keep their salaries but lose the legal right to extra pay for extra hours [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tech employers of salaried IT staff

how_it_helps.text: Rewrites the Fair Labor Standards Act's computer-professional exemption to cover computer network and database analysts, designers, and developers, not just programmers and software engineers [S2][S3].
Sets a bright-line hourly pay threshold of $27.63 for the exemption when workers are paid hourly, and deems exempt workers to be 'professional' employees under the Act [S3].
Defines 'network' to include the Internet, intranets, and the web, which broadens how far the exemption reaches [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The affected computer professionals themselves. Anyone brought inside the exemption loses the federal right to overtime pay after 40 hours a week, so long workweeks cost them income they would otherwise be owed [S2][S3]. The pay threshold limits the reach to relatively well-paid workers, but many database and network specialists near that line would lose overtime eligibility [S3].

drawbacks.text: Workers newly covered by the exemption would lose the right to overtime pay after 40 hours a week, so employers could require longer weeks at no extra cost [S2][S3].
The bill would write the exemption into the statute with a fixed $27.63 hourly threshold, making it harder for the Labor Department to adjust the cutoff over time as wages rise [S3].
The lines between 'skilled' exempt work and routine support work are fuzzy in practice, so some employees doing fairly ordinary network maintenance could arguably be swept into the exemption [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For employers, the bill offers flexibility and lower labor costs; for the workers it covers, the trade is straightforwardly negative, since the only thing the bill changes is the removal of an overtime right [S2][S3]. The high pay threshold means the people affected are relatively well compensated, which softens the impact, but the bill gives those workers nothing in return for what they give up. Writing the threshold into statute rather than leaving it to regulation adds rigidity over time.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which passed it down to a subcommittee, and no further action ever came.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Wilson (R-SC), joined by Rep. Robert Andrews (D-NJ), introduced the bill on May 6, 2003 [S1][S3][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S5].
On May 27, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no markup, floor vote, or further action ever followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The network, database, and systems professionals who would have lost overtime rights are better off that the bill died, since they keep their federal overtime protection. Tech employers are no worse off than before, but did not get the flexibility they would have gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: IT workers who kept overtime rights

for.name: Rep. Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to expand the computer-professional overtime exemption [S1][S5].

for.name: Rep. Robert Andrews
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as the sole Democratic cosponsor [S4][S3].

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 6, 2003 and referred it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections three weeks later; it never held a markup or reported the bill [S5].

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, House Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from May 27, 2003 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2005 without any action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — but the bill never reached a vote, so no party split can be measured.

industries.industry: Technology employers (software, IT services, corporate IT departments)
industries.note: The bill would expand the pool of computer professionals exempt from overtime, letting these employers require longer weeks from network and database staff without time-and-a-half pay [S3]. The industry gains a labor-cost saving that comes directly out of the affected workers' potential earnings [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Network, database, and systems IT workers
industries.note: These are the people the bill would newly exempt from overtime coverage, costing them the federal right to extra pay for hours past 40 a week [S2][S3]. They are relatively well paid — the hourly cutoff is $27.63 — but the exemption is still a pure loss of a protection [S3].
